analysis.one_liner: Gives workers and retirees priority in corporate bankruptcies and limits executive bankruptcy bonuses.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by three Democratic senators, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, vote, or further action before the 115th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite Chapter 11 bankruptcy rules so that employees and retirees recover more of what companies owe them when a business files. It would raise the dollar cap on unpaid wages and benefits that get first claim on a bankrupt company's assets, let unions file creditor claims, and give courts a say in keeping jobs when a company is sold. It would also cut the other way at the top: executives of bankrupt companies could not receive retention bonuses, enhanced retirement benefits, or exit pay while workers' benefits are cut, and courts could claw back compensation paid to directors before a filing.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and retirees of companies in Chapter 11 bankruptcy. They would see doubled priority for unpaid wages and benefits, severance pay treated as a top-of-the-pile administrative expense, protection for retiree health coverage, and damages claims for pension losses when a plan is terminated. Unionized workers would gain the most: unions could file creditor claims, a company could not tear up a union contract without meeting a new strict legal standard, and management cost-cutting would have to be part of a shared sacrifice plan.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and retirees of bankrupt companies

how_it_helps.text: Doubles the bankruptcy priority cap for unpaid wages and benefit claims from $10,000 to $20,000 per employee and removes the 180-day time limit [S3].
Makes severance pay owed to rank-and-file employees an administrative expense paid ahead of most creditors, and gives WARN Act plant-closing damages (up to 60 days' pay) the same status [S3].

Requires a company to negotiate with its union before modifying or rejecting a collective bargaining agreement, and lets a judge reject the request only on clear and convincing evidence that the cuts are the minimum needed to keep the business alive [S3].

Lets active and retired pension participants, and unions, file claims for the shortfall in benefits when a defined benefit pension plan is terminated, and for losses in company stock held in retirement plans when the employer committed fraud [S3].
Requires bankruptcy judges approving a sale of the business to weigh whether the buyer offered to keep existing jobs and assume pension and retiree health obligations [S3].

Bars executives from receiving retention bonuses, enhanced deferred compensation, or retiree benefits while worker or retiree benefits are cut, and requires exit compensation to be court-approved as reasonable and not disproportionate to what nonmanagement workers gave up [S3].
Allows the estate to recover a proportional share of compensation paid to directors in the year before filing, equal to the percentage by which the company cut worker or retiree benefits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Secured lenders and distressed-debt investors, who currently stand first in line in most bankruptcies, would recover less because workers' wage, severance, and benefit claims would jump ahead of theirs and could be charged against their collateral. Executives and consultants of bankrupt companies would face tight caps on bonuses and possible clawbacks. Companies with underfunded pensions and union contracts would find bankruptcy costlier and reorganization slower.

drawbacks.text: Higher priority for wages, severance, and benefit claims means secured lenders recover less from the same pool of assets, and the bill would let those claims be charged against lenders' collateral even if the lender had waived them [S3]. Lenders price that risk, so credit to troubled companies could become more expensive or harder to get.

The new standard for tearing up a union contract — clear and convincing evidence, minimum-necessary cuts, and management cost-sharing — would make reorganizations slower and harder, and a company that cannot renegotiate labor costs may end up liquidating instead of reorganizing, which would cost the jobs the bill aims to save.

Allowing judges to prefer bidders who promise to keep jobs, rather than the highest cash offer, could reduce recoveries for all creditors, including suppliers, pension funds, and small trade creditors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to employees and retirees are concrete and targeted at a documented gap: bankruptcy filings increasingly wipe out worker wages, benefits, and pensions while executive bonus programs continue with little scrutiny [S2, S3]. The costs fall on secured lenders and executives, and the main honest concern is that making bankruptcy more expensive could push some distressed firms into liquidation, which harms workers. Whether that risk outweighs the gains depends on how heavily courts apply the new standards; the bill builds in some flexibility but the compliance burden is real.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, so it died there when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Durbin introduced the bill on March 7, 2018, joined by Senators Whitehouse and Brown [S1, S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary, the only action it ever received [S5].
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or floor action before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Secured lenders and distressed-debt investors, who keep their first-in-line recovery, and executives of bankrupt companies, who keep access to retention bonuses and exit pay without the proposed court review or clawbacks. Workers and retirees of bankrupt companies lost the chance at doubled wage priority, protected severance, and curtailed executive compensation in bankruptcy.

for.name: Sen. Richard Durbin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it to referral to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee (115th Congress)
against.what_they_did: Took no action: no hearing, no markup, no vote, leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Secured lenders and distressed-debt investors
against.role: Primary financial losers under the bill
against.what_they_did: Their priority recoveries and collateral claims would have been reduced by the bill; the bankruptcy finance industry has long opposed measures that subordinate secured creditor recoveries to worker claims.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and both cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and no Republican-led committee took the bill up.

industries.note: The bill would put unpaid wages, severance, and benefits ahead of their recovery from a bankrupt company's assets and would charge some of those claims against their collateral, reducing what they recover. Their gain in the current system is the workers' loss.

industries.industry: Executives and consultants of bankrupt companies
industries.note: Retention bonuses, enhanced deferred compensation, and exit pay would face new court review, caps tied to worker concessions, and possible clawbacks of pay received in the year before filing.
Unions would gain creditor standing to file claims, a strict new standard for rejecting collective bargaining agreements, fee reimbursement, and the right to pursue grievances in bankruptcy.

industries.industry: Companies with underfunded pensions and union contracts
industries.note: Reorganization would become slower and costlier, since claims for pension shortfalls and withdrawal liability would be recognized and labor contracts could be changed only under a stricter standard. Some troubled firms might liquidate instead of reorganizing.
